data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms as a methodological rule for 'verisimilitude-seeking' rather than an inductive probability assignment; it survives by redefining rational action as 'choosing the theory with the highest tested content that has not yet failed,' but this costs the agent any guarantee of predictive reliability or safety, forcing a leap of faith that the future will resemble the past in terms of error-structure.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the agent requires a guarantee of safety (e.g., building a bridge), Popper's framework cannot provide it without smuggling in induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' implies an expectation of future success, then the preference is inductive by definition.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the universe changes its laws tomorrow, the better-corroborated theory offers no logical advantage over a random guess.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'logical probability' (which Popper rejects as increasing with corroboration) and 'methodological preference' (which increases with severity of tests passed). By treating corroboration as a report of past performance without implying future success, the preference becomes a rule for maximizing the potential for learning (falsification) rather than minimizing the risk of being wrong. The surviving theory is preferred not because it is 'more likely true' but because it is the most informative survivor, offering the best target for the next critical test.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
